messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mina Rahman, a 42-year-old project manager, had been healthy and energetic until the winter she was rushed from work with a life-threatening illness that came on with frightening speed. One afternoon she was in a meeting room reviewing deadlines when a wave of cold swept through her body, her skin turned clammy, and by the time she was lying in the emergency department she was seeing drips, needles, and tubes moving toward her arm while the sharp hospital smell filled the air. She remembers the moment in fragments: the bright ceiling lights, someone saying her blood pressure was dropping, and then long stretches that are blank. At other points she has no picture at all, only the full force of terror and helplessness surging through her chest. Even now the story feels so extreme to Mina that she struggles to believe it truly happened to her, and that unreality is part of what makes her mind keep circling it. She had come to believe that her body had been permanently damaged and that her life had been destroyed by the trauma, and when she looked back on the days she was too ill to function she felt she had failed in her most important role in life, unable to protect her family from the chaos that followed. When the antiseptic smell outside a clinic or the sight of needles and IV drips caught her attention, the whole scene of that winter afternoon rushed back at once, not as an idea but as something she felt in her body, with the emergency lights, the cold room, and the blood-pressure alarm all crowding in before she could steady herself.

In the months after discharge, Mina began trying to erase the memory of the event whenever it rose up, pushing away images, filling her days with work, and monitoring her own thoughts for any sign that she was “going crazy.” That effort brought its own consequences. The more she tried to force the memory out, the more it seemed to sharpen in odd pieces, with one minute seeming clear and the next disappearing completely, so that she was left with both jagged details and missing stretches. When she caught a whiff of the antiseptic smell outside a clinic, felt a room turn cold, or saw needles and IV drips in a television scene, the memory came back in a distorted way that made her body react before her mind could organize it. The smell or sight did not just remind Mina of the illness; it seemed to pull the memory apart as it returned, sharpening a flash of bright lights or a blood-pressure alarm one moment and leaving her with blank stretches the next, as if the cue itself were breaking the story into fragments. Those cues were especially potent because they were bound to the worst hours of her illness, and they pulled her into the same emotional intensity even when she could not summon a complete image. Because the memory kept breaking through in that unfinished, vivid way, Mina began to notice new signs of it everywhere: the hiss of the heater, the cold air in a meeting room, or a glimpse of tubing on a cart could suddenly feel like warnings she could not afford to ignore, as if her mind had started scanning the world for anything that resembled that night. Each time this happened she became more convinced that her body had not recovered and that something inside her had been permanently altered. The feeling of failure deepened too: if she could not even sit in a waiting room without panicking, she reasoned, then she was failing again in the role that mattered most to her. She began to read her reactions as proof that her life had been broken beyond repair.

To keep from being overwhelmed, Mina started avoiding hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations. She rearranged her calendar at work to sidestep any medical appointments, and at home she became uneasy whenever the kitchen got too cold or she passed the drawer where her husband kept spare thermometers and first-aid supplies. Because she kept pushing the experience away and refusing to speak about it, the memory never felt settled or stored away; instead, it stayed close and intact, returning with the same force whenever something brushed against it. The harder she worked to avoid thinking about the illness, the more fixed and immediate the memory seemed to become. At the office, when a colleague mentioned a cousin’s surgery or when a delivery rider parked near an ambulance outside the building, she felt her attention snap to her breathing and pulse, scanning herself for signs that her mind was slipping. That constant monitoring made her more alert to every bodily sensation, which in turn made the coldness, smells, and medical images seem even more dangerous and harder to dismiss. Because she was working so hard to keep herself from remembering, the memory often arrived in a stripped-down way, as raw fear without context, and the lack of a coherent picture made it easier for her to believe the illness had left her permanently vulnerable. Once the memory had come back in that jagged, unreal form, Mina started noticing danger everywhere around her: the hiss of the heater, the cold air in a meeting room, even a glimpse of tubing on a cart could set off the same alarm, because anything that resembled the hospital now felt like a possible sign that it was happening again. She took that vulnerability as confirmation that she could no longer trust her body, and the conviction fed back into the thought that her life had been destroyed. Over time she withdrew from routine checkups, delayed seeking care for minor symptoms, and let her husband handle conversations with doctors, even though she knew this was narrowing her world.

By the time Mina sought help, her fear had become tied not only to the hospital itself but to everyday sensations that seemed to echo it, and her marriage had started to feel the strain of her refusals and vigilance. What finally brought her in was a recent episode at work: stepping into a cold conference room, catching the smell of cleaning fluid, and seeing a maintenance cart with tubing and supplies sent her into the same wave of dread that had followed her illness. She left the meeting, sat in her car, and realized she was exhausted from living as though the event were still happening. Mina says she wants to believe her body can be trusted again, but what frightens her most is the thought that one unexpected smell, one cold room, or one glance at a needle could send her straight back into that unreal, devastating night.
